t: Introduction: topic, aim and lesson plan
n: In this topic we study the examination of the body of a fetus and of a newborn. Such an examination is carried out when there are signs of violent death or suspicion of it. The lesson consists of several blocks: signs of being newborn, causes of death in the ante-, intra- and postnatal periods, and establishing live birth. Then we become acquainted with asphyxia. Asphyxia is oxygen deficiency and accumulation of carbon dioxide due to impaired external respiration; if the cause is mechanical, it is called mechanical asphyxia. The final block is devoted to the question of vitality: which signs show that the strangulation furrow and the entry into water occurred during life.

t: Examination of a newborn's body: when and why
n: We consider when and why an examination of a newborn's body is ordered. An examination is ordered in three situations: when the body of a newborn with an unknown mother is found, in stillbirth outside a treatment institution, and when there is a complaint about medical care. The special questions are: whether the infant is newborn, whether it was born alive, what its gestational, that is, fetal, age is, and whether it was viable. If born alive, it is also resolved how long it lived and whether it was cared for. As usual, the cause and time of death, bodily injuries and the mechanism of their infliction are determined.

t: "Newborn": three approaches
n: Now the concept of "newborn". There are three approaches to its duration: 4 weeks in paediatrics, 7 days in obstetrics and gynaecology, and 24 hours in forensic medicine. In forensic medicine this period is closely tied to legislative requirements. Under Article 99 of the Criminal Code, if a mother deliberately kills her child during birth, the punishment is considerably lighter. Attention: Article 99 does not equal Article 97. If another person kills, Article 97 applies, that is, deliberate murder.

t: Signs of being newborn: traces of blood, vernix caseosa
n: The first of the signs of being newborn is traces of blood. If there are no external injuries, finding traces of blood on the body is a sign of being newborn; they arise from rupture of the soft tissues of the birth canal. If the infant's body is washed after birth, the traces of blood disappear. The second sign is vernix caseosa: a whitish-grey semi-liquid mass consisting of sebaceous secretion, desquamated epidermal cells, lanugo and amniotic fluid. In the uterus the vernix protects the skin from maceration by the amniotic fluid. It is more abundant in the folds; if not washed off it persists for up to a week.

t: Distinguishing caput succedaneum from cephalohaematoma
n: We compare caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma. On section of a caput succedaneum, reddish-yellowish serous fluid mixed with blood is seen. It occurs mainly in a narrow pelvis and weak labour; the cause is disturbed circulation from compression in the pelvis, and the site is most often the head, sometimes the buttocks. Its boundary is also found across the projection of the sutures, and it is usually absorbed in 2–3 days. In cephalohaematoma, blood collects under the periosteum; the site is the bones of the cranial vault, limited by the sutures, and it is absorbed over 2 weeks or more. Attention: do not confuse the two; the main difference is the boundary at the suture and the time of absorption.

t: Meconium and the umbilical cord: dynamics of being newborn
n: Now meconium and the umbilical cord. Meconium is a dark green semi-liquid mass; it contains mucus, bile pigments and cells of the intestinal epithelium. It is found on the buttocks, thighs and around the anus; it is usually passed in 1–2 days, in premature infants 3–4 days. The dynamics of the cord are also important. First the cord is moist, shiny and whitish-reddish, then it dries evenly and shrivels. In those born alive, a reddish ring, that is, reactive inflammation, appears at the base of the cord after several hours. After the demarcation ring, the cord falls off in 5–7 days.

t: Absolute and relative signs: distinguishing them
n: We divide the signs into absolute and relative. Absolute signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs; the demarcation ring is absent or only beginning. A cord not separated from the body and placenta is also regarded as an absolutely reliable sign. Relative signs include traces of blood, vernix caseosa and others. Attention: relative signs may also be found on the 2nd day of life and later. Therefore an absolute sign is not equal to a relative sign.

t: Case analysis 1: is it newborn?
n: Case analysis. The body of a newborn with an unknown mother was found. On the body there are traces of blood and vernix caseosa, and the cord is not separated from the body and placenta. Question: which sign is absolute and which relative? Traces of blood and vernix caseosa are relative, while the unseparated cord is absolute. Traces of blood disappear when the body is washed. Vernix caseosa, if not washed off, may persist for up to a week. The basis of the conclusion is this: the unseparated cord is an absolute sign, whereas traces of blood and vernix caseosa are only supplementary, relative evidence.

t: Criteria of live birth and the lung test
n: We turn to the criteria of live birth. WHO criteria: breathing, heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation, voluntary movement. There is no method of detecting heartbeat and movement after death, so mainly it is established whether the infant breathed. The specific gravity of a lung that has not breathed is 1.05–1.06; of one that has breathed, below 1.0, that is, it floats in water. The lung test is done as follows: ligatures are placed and the thoracic organs are put in a vessel of water. If they sink, the result is negative. Then the separate lung, lobe and lobule are tested. If they float, the result is positive and testing is stopped.

t: The lung test: false results and the Taranukhin method
n: False results are possible in the lung test. A false positive result is obtained with putrefactive gases, artificial respiration and frozen lungs not fully thawed. Fragments floated up by putrefactive gas do not float again if squeezed under water. In artificial respiration the floating of fragments is not uniform. A fully thawed frozen lung sinks. A false negative result is obtained in secondary atelectasis. In this case the Taranukhin method (1907), that is, a flask at reduced pressure, or the Trakhtenberg modification (1958), is recommended.

t: Gastrointestinal and radiological tests
n: We consider the other tests. In the Breslau test (1865), on breathing, air passes through the oesophagus into the stomach and intestines. The ligatured organs are put into water, and the parts containing air float. In those born alive, air passes into the gastrointestinal tract gradually. Therefore the test also helps to assess how long the newborn lived. Putrefactive gases and artificial ventilation of the lungs give a false positive, so in such cases this test is not recommended. The radiological test (Dillon, 1939) cannot distinguish a lung that has breathed from artificial ventilation and putrefactive gas. Special equipment is needed, so it is not used in practice.

t: Lung that has breathed and one that has not: macro- and microscopic signs
n: We compare the signs of a lung that has breathed and one that has not. If no breathing occurred, the chest is flat and the diaphragm at the level of the 4th–5th rib; the lung is uniformly bluish dark red, the alveoli are not expanded, and there is no blood in the capillaries. If breathing occurred, the chest is barrel-shaped and the diaphragm at the 6th–7th; the lung is marbled, which is the Bush–Haberda sign; the alveoli are expanded and the capillaries congested. Hyaline membranes are found in those who lived several hours; in a lung that has not breathed they are absent. Lung weight is 55–60 g if there was no breathing; after breathing, circulation begins and it reaches 85–90 g.

t: Quick question 1: tests of live birth
n: Quick question: tests of live birth. In putrefaction, artificial respiration and a frozen lung not fully thawed, the lung test may give a false positive result. Fragments floated up by putrefactive gas do not float again if squeezed under water. A fully thawed frozen lung sinks. In secondary atelectasis the test may be false negative. In this case the Taranukhin method (1907) or the Trakhtenberg modification is recommended. Attention: in putrefaction and artificial respiration, the gastrointestinal test gives a false positive, so it is not recommended.

t: Gestational age: full term, maturity and formulas
n: Now gestational age. Full term: pregnancy on average 10 months, that is, 280 days, 37–42 weeks. Length 50–54 cm, weight 3000–3500 g. A mature fetus has a body length of at least 45 cm and a weight of not less than 2500 g. Attention: full term is not equal to maturity. For the investigation they are important in deciding the duration of pregnancy and viability. Gestational age is calculated by formulas. In Haase's method, in the first half the square root of the body length is taken, for example 16 cm is 4 fetal months. In the second half the body length is divided by 5, and 40 cm is 8 fetal months. By Balthazard–Dervieux the body length is multiplied by 5.6, and 40 cm is 224 days. In Yakupov's method the head circumference is divided by 3.4, and 34 cm is 10 fetal months.

t: Gestational age: ossification centres, cord, placenta
n: Other signs of gestational age. Cord and placenta: in the 6th month 38 cm and 250 g, in the 10th month 50 cm and 500 g. The swallowing reflex appears in the 8th month; the finding of lanugo in meconium is the Shibkov–Markovin sign. Ossification centres are also an indicator of age. The calcaneal centre appears in the 5th fetal month, diameter 0.8–1.1 cm. The talus in the 7th fetal month, diameter 0.7–1.0 cm. The lower femoral epiphysis, that is, the Béclard nucleus, in the 9th fetal month, diameter 0.5–0.7 cm. Pathology of pregnancy and harmful habits delay the centres, and sometimes they may be absent altogether.

t: Viability and signs of care of the infant
n: Viability and signs of care of the infant. By WHO, an infant shorter than 25 cm and lighter than 500 g is non-viable because of extreme prematurity. The body is not opened; only external inspection and measurement of weight and length are done. Attention: live birth is not equal to viability. An infant born alive may also be non-viable. Non-viability is caused by malformations such as anencephaly and a two-chambered heart, and birth trauma incompatible with life, that is, crushing of the brain and fractures of the cervical vertebrae. Signs of care: swaddling and clothing, a cut and tied cord, a body cleaned of blood and vernix caseosa, and milk or a similar mass in the stomach.

t: Duration of life outside the mother's body
n: Duration of life outside the mother's body. Air fills the small intestine in 5–6 hours, and after 6 hours passes into the large intestine. Secondary atelectasis of the lungs develops after not less than 5–6 hours. Meconium is usually passed in 1–2 days. The timeline is as follows: hyaline membranes in 1–2 hours, air in the stomach at less than 3 hours, small intestine at 5–6 hours, demarcation ring at the end of the day, swelling absorbed in 2–3 days. The times are approximate, so many signs are taken into account.

t: Case analysis 2: live birth and duration of life
n: Case analysis: was it born alive and how long did it live? The lung test is positive, air is found only in the stomach, and there are no hyaline membranes in the lungs. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. At least 1–2 hours are necessary for hyaline membranes. Absence of hyaline membranes does not contradict a short life, but by itself does not give an exact time. For the conclusion, false positivity, that is, putrefaction and artificial respiration, is excluded, and the macro- and microscopic signs and the cord ring are assessed.

t: Antenatal and intranatal causes of death
n: Antenatal and intranatal causes of death. Antenatal non-violent death is most often caused by intrauterine asphyxia: placenta praevia, infarction, abruption; cord compression, nuchal cord, true knot. Acute infection of the mother, syphilis, decompensated heart defect, toxaemia of pregnancy and fetal malformations may also lead to death. On the fetal body, signs of rapid death, aspiration of amniotic fluid and a large amount of meconium in it are found; there are often symmetrical haemorrhages in the meninges. In the intranatal period the main cause is birth trauma: fractures of the skull bones, intracranial haemorrhage. A mother giving birth may leave an abrasion with her hand.

t: Postnatal death: non-violent, active and passive killing
n: Postnatal death is of three kinds. Non-violent death is caused by disease or a developmental defect: extreme prematurity, malformations incompatible with life, haemolytic disease, congenital toxoplasmosis, pneumopathy. In active killing, action is taken against the infant: strangulation by hand or ligature, drowning. In passive killing the infant is left without care: bleeding from the cord, cold, hunger. Violent death occurs mainly in the postnatal period; ante- and intranatal violent death is very rare. For law enforcement what matters is not whether it was active or passive, but stating the exact cause of death.

t: Features of examining the body of a fetus and newborn
n: Features of examining the body of a fetus and newborn. In external examination, clothing, swaddling, anthropometry, that is, length, weight, circumference of head, chest and shoulders, and also traces of blood, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum and meconium are assessed. The placenta, that is, weight, shape and tissue, and the cord, that is, length, thickness and knots, are examined. Internal examination begins with the chest and abdomen. The incision of the oral cavity begins from the lower lip; the abdominal incision, so as not to damage the umbilical vessels, runs to both sides short of the umbilicus. The skull is opened with scissors. To establish live birth, floatation tests of the lungs and gastrointestinal tract are done. At the end material is taken for histological and forensic biological examination, that is, blood group.

t: Case analysis 3: period and cause of death
n: Case analysis: period and cause of death. On a fetal body, a large amount of meconium, aspiration of amniotic fluid, and a true knot of the cord are found, and there are no external injuries. Probably non-violent death occurred in the antenatal period from intrauterine asphyxia due to the cord. In birth trauma, by contrast, no external injuries or wounds are formed. The placenta and cord are then examined; the large intestine narrows as meconium is passed; there are often symmetrical haemorrhages in the brain. Question: to which period and which mechanism do these signs correspond? Why are the placenta and cord examined together with the fetal body?

t: Oxygen requirement and tissue sensitivity
n: Now we move on to the topic of asphyxia and first consider the oxygen requirement. 98.5–99.0 % of the oxygen the organism needs is obtained through the respiratory organs, the rest through the skin and gastrointestinal tract. At rest 6–8 l of air per minute are needed; on physical exertion the requirement rises up to 10–20 times. In the central nervous system, cessation of tissue respiration produces an irreversible change in 5–10 minutes; in muscle and connective tissue this period is longer. Normally the oxygen concentration in air is 20.93 %; in hypoxic hypoxia it is lower in the inhaled air.

t: Classification of types of hypoxia
n: Classification of types of hypoxia. Exogenous and endogenous hypoxia are distinguished. Exogenous hypoxia is divided into hypoxic, hyperoxic and hypercapnic. The hypoxic type is seen at low, that is, hypobaric, normal, that is, normobaric, and high, that is, hyperbaric, pressure; the hypercapnic type develops in a confined space. Endogenous hypoxia is respiratory, haemic, circulatory, cytotoxic and physiological. By intensity, fulminant, that is, seconds, acute, that is, minutes, subacute, that is, hours, and chronic hypoxia are distinguished; for forensic medicine the first two are important.

t: Classification of hypoxia, asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia
n: Classification of hypoxia, asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia. Attention: hypoxia is not equal to asphyxia. In asphyxia, oxygen deficiency develops together with an increase in carbon dioxide. "Asphyxia" is a Greek word: a is negation, sphygmos is pulse; the original meaning is absence of pulse. Impairment of external respiration due to a mechanical factor is called mechanical asphyxia; it is divided into three types: from compression, that is, strangulation and compression; from obstruction, that is, obstruction of the respiratory openings and airways, and drowning; and in a confined space, where oxygen decreases and CO₂ increases. A special case is autoerotic asphyxiation, that is, sexual asphyxia, usually an accident.

t: Autoerotic asphyxiation (sexual asphyxia)
n: Autoerotic asphyxiation, that is, sexual asphyxia. This is a state in which sexual arousal occurs under conditions of hypoxia and hypercapnia. It is more common in solitary middle-aged men prone to sexual deviations, sometimes in young men. The asphyxial process is regulated with the help of hands, feet and devices: the neck is compressed with a ligature or a polyethylene bag is used. If this ends in death, it is assessed as an accident; the scene should be inspected carefully.

t: Course of asphyxia during life: stages
n: We consider the stages of the course of asphyxia during life. In the preasphyxial period the organism mobilises its compensatory capacities, so signs of asphyxia do not yet develop; this period lasts 20–30 sec. Then inspiratory dyspnoea lasts about 1 min, and expiratory dyspnoea also about 1 min. In the inspiratory stage consciousness is lost within 40–60 sec.; in the expiratory stage clonic convulsions with passage of urine and faeces are possible. Respiratory arrest lasts 30–40 sec. Terminal breathing continues up to 5 minutes; after breathing stops the heart may beat for another 3–10 minutes.

t: Postasphyxial state: periods and consequences
n: The postasphyxial state is the set of changes that develop in those who survive asphyxia. It consists of four periods: asphyxial coma, stupor, disorientation and amnesia, and residual effects. In the first minutes and hours death occurs from asphyxial coma. In the first day the cause of death is oedema of the lungs and brain, and later hypostatic pneumonia.

t: General signs of mechanical asphyxia
n: General signs of mechanical asphyxia. External signs: cyanosis, cadaveric lividity, mydriasis, subconjunctival ecchymoses. Cyanosis and mydriasis are inconstant, and ecchymoses appear in the dyspnoeic stage. Internal signs: fluid blood, the asphyxial heart, in which the right chambers are full of blood, Tardieu spots and a shrunken spleen, that is, Sabinsky's sign. These signs are not specific for mechanical asphyxia and occur in other kinds of rapid death too. In diagnosis the signs are assessed not singly but as a whole. The asphyxial heart, anaemia and shrunken spleen are regarded as relatively pathognomonic.

t: Quick question 2: general asphyxial signs
n: A quick question on the general asphyxial signs. Where and at what stage do Tardieu spots form? Answer: dark red haemorrhages 2–3 mm under the visceral pleura and epicardium; in inspiratory dyspnoea; between the lung lobes, on the diaphragmatic pleura. Which signs are relatively pathognomonic? The asphyxial heart, anaemia, shrunken spleen, that is, Sabinsky's sign; the blood in the spleen leaves the depot in the preasphyxial period. Attention: Tardieu spots are not equal to Rasskazov–Lukomsky–Paltauf spots. The latter form in true drowning and are not found under the epicardium.

t: Hanging: mechanism of death and strangulation furrow
n: Hanging: mechanism of death and strangulation furrow. In typical hanging the body hangs freely in the ligature, in atypical hanging part of the body has support. Factors of death: narrowing of the airway, compression of veins, nervous reflex, sometimes rupture of the spinal cord. In typical hanging the furrow is above the hyoid bone and obliquely vertical; in atypical hanging it is lower. The furrow depends on the material of the ligature. From a rigid ligature, for example wire or chain, the furrow is firmer and deeper. From a soft ligature, towel or scarf, the skin furrow is not pronounced, while on internal examination there is the "copper wire" sign (Casper). On the side opposite the knot the furrow is more pronounced and deeper.

t: Signs for establishing the vitality of the furrow
n: Signs for establishing the vitality of the furrow. In disputed cases it is important to establish the vitality of the furrow; in the Bocarius test a skin flap is examined against the light. Congestion and haemorrhage in the ridge indicate vitality; under the microscope Neiding's sign shows circulatory disturbance, and Kasyanov's sign reactive inflammation. With a soft ligature there is a whitish streak in the projection of the furrow, that is, the "copper wire" sign (Casper); haemorrhage behind the larynx is Brouardel's sign. Signs of stretching: Amussat, rupture of the intima of the carotid artery; Martin, blood in the outer coat of the artery; Walcher, blood at the lower end of the muscle; Simon, blood in the disc.

t: Ligature, manual and blunt-object strangulation: differences
n: We distinguish hanging from ligature strangulation. In manual strangulation, finger bruises, fingernail abrasions and internal injuries, that is, injury of bone and cartilage, are pronounced. With a blunt object, the injury lies in the projection of the contact surface: bruise, abrasion, injury of the hyoid bone. In hanging the furrow is obliquely vertical, high on the neck; signs of stretching such as Amussat, Walcher and Simon may be present; facial cyanosis and lividity are comparatively less marked. In ligature strangulation the furrow is horizontal, at the level of the cartilage and lower; signs of stretching do not arise; fracture of the horns of the cartilage is possible; facial cyanosis and lividity are more marked. In positional asphyxia there is no furrow; the diagnosis is made by excluding other causes of death.

t: Obstructive asphyxia: respiratory openings and airways
n: Obstructive asphyxia, that is, obstruction of the respiratory openings and airways. When the respiratory openings are closed and there was no resistance, there are no changes other than the general asphyxial signs. With resistance, bruises and abrasions occur around the mouth and nose. The airways are obstructed by a foreign body, for example a fruit stone or button, by a pourable substance, for example sand or flour, and by a liquid, for example blood or vomit. This is most often an accident. Mechanism of death: difficulty in the passage of air, reflex spasm of the vocal cords, or reflex cardiac arrest; the signs may not form. Attention: vomit in the airways is not always asphyxia. In massage, transportation and putrefaction the mass is small and does not reach the small bronchi.

t: True and asphyxial drowning: comparison table
n: We compare true and asphyxial drowning. In true drowning the froth is persistent and fine-bubbled, which is Krushevsky's sign; in asphyxial drowning it is scanty and unstable. In true drowning water reaches the alveoli, the lungs are doughy, Rasskazov–Lukomsky–Paltauf spots lie under the pleura, haemodilution and haemolysis are observed, and up to 300 ml of water is found in the stomach. In asphyxial drowning water does not reach the alveoli, emphysema is sharp, only Tardieu spots lie under the pleura, there is no haemodilution, and the stomach may contain up to 1 l of water. In asphyxial drowning there is air embolism of the heart; in the Sunsov test the left ventricle is punctured. In salt water the blood thickens and Rasskazov–Lukomsky–Paltauf spots do not form.

t: Vitality of drowning and signs of immersion in water
n: Vitality of drowning and signs of immersion in water. In true drowning, diatom plankton is found in parenchymatous organs and bone marrow; it must correspond to the body of water. A finding in the lungs alone is of no significance. Additional methods: pseudoplankton, water bacteria, cryoscopic and refractometric. In reflex arrest on entering water, signs of asphyxia do not develop. After hours the fingers wrinkle; at 2–5 days the "washerwoman's hand", at 2–3 weeks the "glove of death", at 10–15 days the hair is easily pulled out. Attention: these changes do not show the cause of death. In a newborn the vernix caseosa protects the skin from maceration.

t: Duration of immersion in water: skin changes
n: The duration of immersion of a body in water is assessed from skin changes. After several hours the fingers and toes pale and wrinkle; at 2–5 days the change involves the palmar surface. At 5–8 days the plantar surface is fully involved; the changes of the limbs take on the appearance of the "washerwoman's hand". After 2–3 weeks the skin of the palms with the nails may separate in the form of "gloves of death" and "stockings of death". At 10–15 days the hair is easily pulled out. The changes depend on water temperature, clothing and age, and do not show the cause of death.

t: Compression asphyxia and asphyxia in a confined space
n: Compression asphyxia and asphyxia in a confined space. Compression asphyxia occurs when the chest and abdomen are compressed by blunt objects and respiratory movement is restricted; more often in earthquakes, collapses and crowds. Frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. If the chest and abdomen are compressed simultaneously, the movement of the lungs, heart and diaphragm is disturbed; the abdomen is more resistant to compression. Characteristic signs: swelling and blueness of the face, haemorrhages on the face, neck and chest, the "ecchymotic mask" (Olive–Danger); "carmine swelling" of the lungs (Lacassagne). In a confined space oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases. The dangerous limit is 2.0–2.5 % in children and 8–10 % in adults; there are no specific signs.

t: Case analysis 4: type and vitality of asphyxia
n: Case analysis: type and vitality of asphyxia. A body was recovered from a body of water. Around the mouth and nose there is fine-bubbled white froth, in the airways foreign substances, and in the stomach water. In true drowning water reaches the alveoli and there is persistent fine-bubbled white froth, that is, Krushevsky's sign; up to 300 ml of water in the stomach, which is Fegerlund's sign. In asphyxial drowning, because of laryngospasm, water does not enter the airways and no foreign substances are found; the stomach may contain up to 1 l of water. Question: which type? Vitality is confirmed by diatom plankton: if it is found in the organs and bone marrow and corresponds to the water of the body of water. A finding in the lungs is of no significance.

t: Conclusion: main theses and review questions
n: We conclude. Newborn status is the first 24 hours. Absolute signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence of the demarcation ring or its initial signs, and an unseparated cord. Live birth is resolved mainly by whether the infant breathed: lung and gastrointestinal tests and macro- and microscopic examination are carried out. Antenatal death is more often caused by asphyxia connected with the placenta and cord; intranatal death by birth trauma; violent death mainly in the postnatal period. The general asphyxial signs, for example Tardieu spots, are not specific, and their whole set is assessed. The vitality of drowning is confirmed by examination of diatom plankton.
